Upside Foods can now make a million pounds of chicken a year without killing any animals

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, upside Foods didn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet.
  • The eleven-year-old company had undergone a 10,000-fold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry.
  • So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself, taste-testing two chicken sandwiches on camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, upside Foods didn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet. The YouTuber revealed up at the manufacturer’s facility with his video crew.

The eleven-year-old company had undergone a 10,000-fold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry. Upside notes it can now make over one million pounds of edible, cultivated chicken each year without killing a single animal in the process. Such an achievement challenges the long-held industry skepticism over whether lab-grown meat will ever be affordable enough to meaningfully scale.

So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself, taste-testing two chicken sandwiches on camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken. He was unable to identify which sandwich was which — they tasted exactly the same to him.

“I mean, you see me in the video – I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, what is he going to say?’” Upside Foods CEO Dr. Uma Valeti told TechCrunch. “I thought he would maybe say a nice thing here and there, but he would get it right. But he didn’t.”.

Sources indicate that if there was any reason to doubt Donaldson’s assessment, now you can taste the chicken yourself, if you live in California. Upside Foods announced on Tuesday that it will now be available at several restaurants in the state, marking a major milestone for the cultivated meat industry.

Industry observers note that “This has been a decade of foundation building,” Valeti stated, adding that Upside Foods has secured its next set of regulatory approvals from the FDA and USDA. “With that comes the whole excitement and ice-breaking for the field … There’s brilliant ideas in science, but science only makes an impact when you get to scale.”.

It has been revealed that solving this scale problem has been the biggest obstacle for the cultivated meat industry. The first ever lab-grown hamburger, produced in 2013, cost $300,000 to make. Now, Valeti says that Upside Foods can match the price range of “really high quality organic chicken.”.

“The whole industry was going through this really difficult scale-up period… We had to go through that grinder to come out on the other side,” Valeti said.

The cultivated meat movement isn’t just about animal welfare (though for many, that’s a plus). According to the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit think tank for alternative proteins, it would take 5.5 Earths to feed the world with conventional meat production in 2050, when the United Nations predicts that the global population will approach 10 billion.

In a recent development, “We use less water, less land, less energy,” Valeti said. “The power of this technology is you protect the choice of eating what we love, but we can also protect everything else we love about protecting life, and the environment, and animal welfare.”.

The process of cultivating meat also cuts the risk of E. coli, Salmonella, and antibiotic resistance while lowering cholesterol and saturated fat, the manufacturer promises. Upside Foods’ chicken is also augmented with soy protein isolate, pea fiber, and olive oil, making it more nutritionally dense. Valeti says that this doesn’t affect the flavor, which is something he agonized over. He even brought in Michelin-starred and James Beard Award-winning chefs, Thomas Keller and Nancy Silverton, to weigh in on the taste.

“We got a lot of confidence after we worked with [these chefs],” Valeti stated. “They said, ‘Uma, you and your team are obsessing too much about it. The majority of people, when you put this in your chicken dishes, will not be able to tell.’”.

According to recent reports, upside Foods’ milestone of producing one million pounds of chicken per year is meaningful, but the industry still has a long way to go. In 2021, it was estimated that Americans consume about 8 billion chickens annually. But aside from sheer capital, Valeti believes the firm has been able to scale the amount it has because of how much it has learned by experimenting with the process over the years. He thinks more growth is possible.

“Unless we show it at the largest scale possible that anybody has done, no one is going to believe us,” he remarked.

Breaking: The Verge Best of 2026

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The top 25 products of the year as selected by our staff.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
  • The top 25 products of the year as selected by our staff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The top 25 products of the year as selected by our staff.

Recent findings suggest that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The top 25 products of the year as selected by our staff.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Hundreds of gadgets pass across our desks each year. Some leave their mark and get a full review or make it to the top of a buying guide. It’s harder than it sounds to narrow down our favorites. Instead of simply picking products that scored highly, or only those that made it into our buying guides, we asked our reviews team and staff at large to nominate their products of the year. Then our editors whittled the list down to the top 25, balancing categories like smart home, phones, laptops, and just cool stuff.

The result is our Best of 2026 — a list of products our staff has purchased, reviewed, or just plain loves. It’s still mid-November, and we know latest products are set to launch before the end of the year. So we may upgrade this list if there’s anything we think deserves a spot before the ball drops on New Year’s Eve. Then we dive right into CES and start all over again in 2027.

Without further ado… here are The Verge Best of 2026 winners.

According to recent reports, the Saros 20 is one of Roborock’s current flagship floor cleaners, but it distinguishes itself from the rest of the manufacturer’s robovacs with a pair of extending leglike appendages on the underside. It uses those legs to boost itself over obstacles, like uneven transitions between rooms. It’s highly maneuverable, thanks to its use of spinning mop pads instead of a heavy roller, and without a lidar tower protruding out the top. The Saros 20 is just 3.13 inches tall, small enough to squeeze under most furniture. It’s also equipped with excellent obstacle avoidance, and it uses a split brush design underneath with a gap, allowing hair and fibers to get quickly sucked instead of tangled up in bristles. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

The Navimow X430 came out on top of our robot lawnmower showdown earlier this year, and The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy said it was “by far” the best one she tested. It was the only one that could mow her front and back yards in one trip, and the only one that didn’t get stuck. It even successfully rolled through potholes and over small tree branches. The Navimow X430’s 17-inch cutting width was also wider than the competition, helping it finish mowing faster. It navigates using a combination of technologies, but there’s also a handy remote control mode you can use to take over in sensitive spots in your yard, or to clean up stray grass fronds the bot missed. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer.

Sources indicate that the Fairphone 6 Plus is just a regular old Android phone, and that’s actually a triumph. Fairphone has been selling its repairable, ethically sourced phones for years now, and previous generations have been underpowered or come with serious compromises. The Fairphone 6 Plus doesn’t feel compromised in the same way, and it comes with swappable back panels with different accessories, like a wallet or grip. The $649 price feels entirely reasonable for what it offers, especially when you consider that you can take care of easy fixes, like swapping in a new battery yourself at minimal cost. In a year when we got a lot of bad RAMageddon-related news in the smartphone industry, the Fairphone 6 Plus felt like a relief. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max easily secured a spot on our Best of 2026 list. Apple didn’t change much in its winning formula this year but focused on what people care about most: camera and battery life. The biggest enhancement is probably the main camera, which now has a variable aperture that lets photographers adjust background blur and take better low-light photos. The iPhone 18 Pro Max also has the longest battery life in an iPhone to date, while the iPhone 18 Pro lasts as long as last year’s 17 Pro Max. — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor.

It has been revealed that before there was the iPhone Duo, there was the Z Fold 8. Not by much — just a few months — but Samsung beat Apple to market with a passport-shaped foldable. It’s a little thinner, lighter, and narrower than the Duo, and that makes a real difference in how comfortable it is to use for long stretches of time. It’s not rated for the same level of dust resistance as the Duo, and it doesn’t feel quite as “premium,” but apps make better use of the cover screen. The more I hold it, the more I think Apple needs to take a page out of Samsung’s book here. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer.

Industry observers note that 3D printing is finally something I can recommend to just about anyone with space for a 30-inch cube in their garage, because the Bambu Lab P2S Combo is the easiest printing experience I’ve touched. It prints beautifully out of the box but, more importantly, it keeps on printing with minimal care, maintenance, or fuss. I can leave rolls of colorful filament inside for months, then press a button on my phone to print, because the bundled AMS keeps them dry and automatically loads each one. Technically the P2S arrived in 2025, but I’d never buy a just-released 3D printer: I spent a year and over 1,700 hours of print time (and counting) to be sure of my recommendation. Wish Bambu treated the open-source community better, though. — Sean Hollister, senior editor.

According to recent reports, when The Verge decided to do a Best of 2026, my mind immediately jumped to the nerdiest thing I’ve tested all year — a dongle that lets you power aging gadgets with the same USB-C cables that charge your laptop and phone. Lose your SNES power brick? Want to make a desktop monitor portable? Want to make a Game Boy run forever? Werewolf VFLEX can make those happen, and so much more. It’s like having a universal AC adapter, one you don’t even need to plug into the wall, because USB-C batteries are amazing. — Sean Hollister, senior editor.

In a recent development, it’s no surprise that, given its provenance, the Fitbit Air is an excellent fitness tracker, even if its tracking capabilities don’t go as in depth as other devices. For $100, the Air comes with a thinner and more comfortable strap than Whoop’s bands, with a design that lets the sensor module be easily removed and swapped into other straps. Battery life is excellent, requiring just a handful of charges each month while the Air tracks metrics like steps, heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and cardio load. All of that data is available through the Google Health app without a subscription, but for $100 you can upgrade to Google Health Premium, which adds access to video workouts, adaptive fitness aims, and an AI health coach that can share summaries of your day or night and answer questions about your health. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

I usually regret my TikTok shop purchases. Not this one. I was tired of filling my journals with muddy, blue-tinged photos from HP Sprocket that faded over time. The Liene Pearl N200 Pro uses dye sublimation, so the colors are super vivid. The app is easy to use, and it comes with 50 sheets and five ink cartridges. You can usually find it for $100 to $120, and refills cost just $25 for 50 sheets. That’s pretty affordable — especially if you love scrapbooking. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer.

Recent findings suggest that the Oura Ring 5 is thinner and lighter than the Oura Ring 4. The metal finish is more durable than Oura’s previous models, so nicks and scratches should be less of an matter. The case also adds support for on-the-go wireless charging, but unfortunately it’s sold separately. This year’s Oura Ring also dropped the smallest and largest size options. The Oura Ring 5 is still the best smart ring on the market, especially if you’re upgrading from an older model or are new to smart rings. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer.

It has been revealed that 2026 is the year nearly every TV manufacturer released an RGB LED TV, which uses individual red, green, and blue LEDs to provide the backlight instead of a field of blue or white LEDs. The Sony Bravia 9 II is the best of the bunch, with accurate, vibrant color; the incredible processing that Sony is known for; and a really cool lenticular screen on the stand that hides the cables behind it. The first generation of a new technology is always a bit tricky, but Sony indicated that an RGB LED TV can be done right. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer.

It has been revealed that when Sony launched its WH-1000XM4C wireless headphones in October, there was a certain amount of smug satisfaction enjoyed by those of us who still prefer Sony’s six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones over its successors. Sony made significant design changes with the WH-1000XM5 and then walked a few of them back with the WH-1000XM6. Both have better active noise cancellation and battery life than Sony’s latest, but the newly introduced XM4C resurrects the XM4’s comfortable, compact folding design with a replaceable battery, so loyal fans of the original can enjoy the new version for years to come. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

The Liberty 5 Pro set a new bar for call quality this year. The Verge’s John Higgins noted they delivered the best in-call noise canceling he’s ever heard, even compared with pricier headphones like Apple’s AirPods Pro 3. They run on Anker’s new Thus chip and feature 9.2mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and IP55 water resistance. The case also has a built-in display to rapidly change settings like ANC or check the Liberty 5 Pro’s battery life, with separate icons for each earbud and the case itself. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer.

There’s plenty about the Studio Display XDR to find interesting: It’s the first Apple 5K monitor with a mini-LED panel and quantum dots that has a peak brightness of 2,000 nits, it has an adaptive refresh rate up to 120Hz, and it has a bunch of color-accurate reference modes for a wide range of professional uses. But what got me most excited was the inclusion of Apple’s CMF 2026 color-matching function for its two general picture-mode presets. It’s a latest display standard developed as an alternative to CIE 1931, the standard for the past 80 years, which can cause colors to look different across multiple narrow-band display technologies like OLED and mini-LED with quantum dots. Apple CMF 2026 aims to fix that, and I’m here for it. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer.

The MacBook Neo, despite running on an iPhone chip, works pretty darn well as a MacBook, and that’s mostly all I need to say. Yes, it now starts at $699 instead of $599 because of RAMageddon, so it’s not as good of a deal as it was when it released. But it’s a very functional laptop, still has a great keyboard and (mechanical!) trackpad, and comes in fun colors. Apple hit it out of the park with the Neo. — Jay Peters, senior reporter.

According to recent reports, framework’s Laptop 13 Pro is my ideal all-purpose Windows laptop (or Linux, if you’re inclined). It’s portable, powerful, dabbles in 1080p gaming, and it’s even user-upgradable and repairable. It’s the Framework formula many of us have come to love, like those precious modular ports, but with a major step up in quality-of-life features: a haptic trackpad, a nice touchscreen, and a much-improved build. Its biggest fault is its price. That’s the toll RAMageddon has taken on everything this year — it just hit a smaller manufacturer like Framework harder. Yes, Framework chose an extra-pricey component in LPCAMM2 memory, but that’s also part of why the 13 Pro is so cool and forward-looking. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

Sources indicate that I was so head over heels for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome when I reviewed it that I recently bought one. A black-and-white-only fixed-lens camera is super niche, but for this photo nerd, it’s the perfect “artsy” pocket camera. I take it with me everywhere, even with my larger cameras during Verge events or wedding shoots. It’s a palate cleanser for everything from slice-of-life family snapshots to Latest York City street photography. I could achieve that with black-and-white film, but I inevitably fall off using my analog cameras. They say the best camera is the one you have with you, and the GR IV Monochrome is now always with me and always a delight. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

The Nape Pro is the most unusual and best gadget I bought this year. It’s a bar-shaped device with six customizable buttons and a small trackball in the middle. I put it horizontally below my space bar, and once I tweaked the button layout, it became a daily driver. It feels like a cross between a trackpad and what I wish the TrackPoint on my ThinkPad was. The Nape Pro works over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz and supports up to 1000Hz polling. Battery life is fantastic, and it’s fully customizable. I still use a mouse at the significant desk, but the Nape Pro is now as vital to my portable setup as my laptop stand and keyboard. — Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor.

In a recent development, xteink redefined how small an e-reader can be, and while the company released several models in 2026 — including the X3, X4, and X4 Classic — the X4 Pro is the best of the bunch. It’s the company’s only model to include lighting and a touchscreen, which makes navigating Xteink’s software, or an excellent third-party alternative, much easier than using buttons alone. At $99, the X4 Pro is Xteink’s most expensive e-reader, and it doesn’t include access to an online bookstore, but with a 4.26-inch screen, you can slip it in a pocket alongside your phone. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

Months after reviewing it, I’m still a huge fan of Valve’s second-generation Steam Controller. It’s comfortable to hold for hours-long gaming sessions, has enough battery life that I never really think about it, and I love how I can customize nearly everything about the controller on a per-game basis inside Steam. If I have one knock against the controller, it’s that I don’t use the significant touchpads all that often to replicate a mouse — but I have used them as giant buttons, which can be surprisingly useful in a pinch. I think I’ll be gaming with it for years to come.— Jay Peters, senior reporter.

The Peak Design City Bags offer a unique way to hang them up wherever you are. They have a hook so you can hang them off a table and keep them off the dirty ground. The Verge’s Thomas Ricker, who reviewed the bags, said they made him a convert: “It beats setting a bag on the dirty ground or hanging it off the back of the chair where it will inevitably slide onto the floor, and it’s far better than holding a bag on your sweaty lap on a hot summer day.” He said they fit squarely in the everyday carry sweet spot for most people. — Jay Peters, senior reporter.

Industry observers note that I love ridiculous laptops, and there’s nothing quite as over-the-top as dual-screen models like Asus’ Zephyrus Duo and Zenbook Duo. The wildly expensive Zephyrus Duo gaming laptop is the perfect embodiment of this extravagant formula, with a mobile RTX 5090 GPU, dual 16-inch OLEDs, and a $5,500 price tag. It’s a marvel of maximalism. The more practical version is the latest Zenbook Duo — with its pair of 14-inch OLEDs and Intel Panther Lake chip — which is still pricey at $2,700, but no slouch for 1080p gaming on its integrated GPU. I wish these kinds of laptops had more accessible price points because they are an absolute treat to use. The more screens, the merrier. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

Industry observers note that the Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 power bank is the latest update in its line of ultralight battery packs. Nitecore has made a name for itself among endurance athletes and backpackers who want to pack as light as possible while still having enough power to recharge a phone and a smartwatch. The NB10000 has IPX7 protection to withstand rain or light immersion, two USB-C ports, a 10,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, and enough juice to top up an iPhone 15 Pro twice. It costs $84, which is a lot more than what you’d spend on a standard 10,000mAh battery, but it’s worth it for anyone who wants a thin and light battery that lasts. Oh, and did we mention there are RGB lights around the USB-C ports? — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor.

In a recent development, few products are truly perfect all-rounders in the smart home world, but Aqara’s G400 video doorbell comes close. It works with every platform, has local storage, and offers on-device AI to alert you to people at your door. It can record 24/7 because it’s hardwired, which also makes it a good choice for reliability, and there’s even the option of power over ethernet. It looks like a giant Mars bar on my front door, but I can forgive it for this because it does everything else very well. And at only $100, it is one of those rarities in tech today: a good product that’s affordable. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer.

The Schlage Sense Pro is the smartest lock on the block, thanks to ultra-wideband hands-free unlocking. With your phone in your pocket or bag, it can unlock as you approach, so you can just open the door — no need for keys or fiddling with an app. It’s like stepping into the future. While there are a couple of other UWB locks out there, the Schlage is my favorite because of its sleek, all-metal design, lack of a keyhole, and a very discreet keypad. Today, it works only with Apple Home Key for that magical unlocking, but thanks to its support for Aliro, the new smart lock standard, it should work with Android phones very soon. Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer.

Genesis AI raises $500 million to deploy glove-wearing robots

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Genesis AI has “cracked dexterous manipulation,” CEO and co-founder Zhou Xian notes.
  • According to recent reports, to make his case, Xian hosted TechCrunch at Genesis AI’s Silicon Valley facility, where its physical AI model operated a pair of off-the-shelf robotic arms.
  • It’s an impressive demo, exactly the kind of complex workflow that today’s robots struggle to complete.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Genesis AI has “cracked dexterous manipulation,” CEO and co-founder Zhou Xian notes.

According to recent reports, to make his case, Xian hosted TechCrunch at Genesis AI’s Silicon Valley facility, where its physical AI model operated a pair of off-the-shelf robotic arms. In one demo, the arms picked up two small cardboard boxes, scanned them, placed them in a larger cardboard box, folded it closed, taped it shut, and then plucked a label off a strip of printer tape and applied it to the box.

It’s an impressive demo, exactly the kind of complex workflow that today’s robots struggle to complete. And while Genesis wouldn’t let your reporter mess with the robot’s mise en place to test its wiles, the firm did agree to re-run the presentation. During the second go-round, the robot fumbled a box and had a heck of a time peeling the tiny adhesive label off the printer tape. A mistake, but also the kind of edge case that can be used to improve a model—”hiccup data,” a Genesis executive suggests.

According to recent reports, this is the exact gap—between a lab demo and reliable automation—that Genesis, and the rest of the humanoid physical AI ecosystem, need to bridge if they want to avoid another robot winter. To do so, Xian’s tech giant is announcing a $500 million Series A round led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest, and Eclipse.

It has been revealed that xian and Genesis president Théophile Gervet, who met as graduate students in a Carnegie Mellon University lab, cofounded the tech giant in 2024. Genesis revealed its $105 million seed round in July 2025. The company’s strategy is vertical integration: generating the bulk of its own training data, developing its own generative AI model, and doing both in concert with the design and construction of a humanoid robot.

“We wanted to ship the best robot, end-to-end product,” Xian stated.

Recent findings suggest that the startup’s focus on dexterity — the robot’s ability to do stuff with its hands — and gathering the right data to achieve it sets it apart from competitors like Figure or Agility. Genesis gathers force data (apparently the unlock for effective manipulation) using a sensor-enabled glove. The gloves, and accompanying headset cameras, are worn by more than 100 real workers around the world, whose activities contribute to a training dataset that feeds into the company’s model.

The company’s robots wear the same sensor-equipped gloves, and their “hands” are designed to mimic the proportions of human hands. That fidelity, Xian says, enables the robots’ capabilities in sorting and wire manipulation.

Sources indicate that the other big investment the tech giant has made is in simulation. One of its advisers, Minchen Li, is a co-author of an influential physics algorithm used by the startup to create millions of high-fidelity models of the robot’s experience.

In a recent development, still, about that robot: Xian said that the organization’s model was more capable when operating Eno, the company’s flagship humanoid robot. But Eno wasn’t ready to demonstrate its abilities for TechCrunch.

A handsome machine bearing more than a hint of the late Steve Jobs’ influence on tech gadgets and their marketing, Eno reflects “the feeling” the company wants to deliver to its customers. That means less of a Terminator-styled metal skeleton and more of an iMac on wheels.

Industry observers note that genesis mentioned it has built 30 to 40 Enos, but wasn’t ready to share how many it would make in the year ahead. The manufacturer would only say that a mass-manufacturing contractor had been chosen to start work next year in the U.S. and that the design of the mass-produced version had been finalized. The company is piloting the machine with a handful of undisclosed customers.

Industry observers note that to realize the tech giant’s vision, Xian says the key bottleneck is hardware capability, both in mechanical design and in the supply chains needed to produce industrial-grade machines. Right now, the company’s dexterous hands can only operate for a few weeks of regular work before they need to be replaced.

Recent findings suggest that for truly generalized robotic intelligence, Genesis needs more data. Xian pooh-poohs the finer distinctions between architectures like Vision-Language-Action models and World-Action models. In his view, the software is ultimately transformers and attention, so “what really matters is is the whole infra — the training infrastructure, the data infrastructure, and the quality of the data.” He estimates that “the model architecture contributes to maybe 10% of of the final [result].”.

“I don’t think we expect or we need another fundamental scientific leap,” he told TechCrunch. “No, we have all the recipes. It’s just about execution.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A press release explained that Jet Lag Strategy was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore.
  • In a recent development, jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for owners who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, traveling to newly introduced places is good for the soul, but then there’s jet lag, which can cause fatigue, headaches, insomnia and even nausea during your trip. Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, wants to help you combat these effects with its latest feature, Jet Lag Strategy, which launched on Tuesday.

A press release explained that Jet Lag Strategy was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore. The study analyzed de-identified data covering 1.5 million nights of sleep from over 57,000 Oura members to determine how sleep shifted before and after about 65,000 long-distance trips.

In a recent development, jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for owners who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype. The latter describes whether you’re a morning person, a night person or somewhere in between.

Recent findings suggest that oura uses 40 to 90 days of sleep timing and activity and average body temperature trends to assign customers one of six chronotypes: early morning type, morning type, late morning type, early evening type, evening type and late evening type. This can change over time.

Both your chronotype and sleep history also inform your circadian low point. Usually around 4 a.m., this is when your body temperature is at its lowest and you’re the most ready for sleep.

In the Oura app, you can start a Jet Lag Blueprint in one of four ways: by adding travel from the Today tab, selecting “Jet Lag” from the app menu, asking the AI-powered Oura Advisor to create a plan for your upcoming trip or responding to a prompt when Oura detects that your phone has changed time zones.

In addition to your flight details, you’ll also want to share the reason for your trip, as a work-related Jet Lag Initiative will differ from a vacation one.

Sources indicate that your Jet Lag Proposal will then populate with a recommended schedule for sleep, caffeine, activity and light exposure before, during and after your trip, with reminders and the ability to mark actions as complete. You can request adjustments to this plan using Oura Advisor.

According to recent reports, during your trip, you’ll be able to compare your readiness score to the typical score for similar trips. This is based on data from 10 million trips already taken by Oura members.

Once your trip ends, you’ll receive a report comparing your sleep and readiness scores before and during your trip.

Jet Lag Plan is now available to Oura members whose language is set to English. It works with an Oura Ring 3 or newer on both Android and iOS.

The latest Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, while a membership is $6 per month or $70 per year.

It has been revealed that the information contained in this article is for educational and informational purposes only and is not intended as health or medical advice. Always consult a physician or other qualified health provider regarding any questions you may have about a medical condition or health objectives.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around Latest York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

It has been revealed that to children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

She’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso stated in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”.

Sources indicate that talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.
  • Uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.

Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.

Uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday. The initial rollout begins in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, with Dallas next in line and dozens of additional US cities planned.

Recent findings suggest that the rollout comes after Uber and Zipline first announced their tie-up, including an investment in Zipline by Uber, back in August 2026. The companies have set the ambitious goal to hit 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029.

It has been revealed that spring residents in the coverage area will see a newly introduced “Drone” icon in the Uber app’s home screen to browse participating restaurants. At checkout, customers will need to confirm a clear drop-off zone in the yard, and can track the drone in real-time via the app. Because the system is fully autonomous, tipping is disabled — though customers can still rate the experience in the app.

Unlike other low-hovering delivery drones, Zipline’s aircraft cruise at over 300 feet at speeds up to 70 mph. The drone hovers high overhead and lowers a tethered delivery pod onto the customer’s doorstep or yard. The drones dynamically calculate flight paths based on wind, altitude, and speed — dipping their noses to accelerate or pitching upward to brake as quietly as possible. The drones are built to fly in rain and poor weather, carrying up to 8 pounds of cargo within a 10-mile radius of the restaurant.

The initial plan is to operate daily from 8AM to 10PM, Uber indicates. Customers can order from national chains like Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, alongside dozens of Houston-area staples such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal.

To be sure, the “1 million deliveries a day by 2029” target is very aggressive, especially considering that Zipline presently averages roughly one delivery every 20 seconds globally, or around 4,300 a day. Still, delivery drones are becoming a more widely adopted technology in many communities across the US, with Uber competing alongside other players like Amazon Prime Air and Google-backed Wing.

Latest Update: Spotify’s fresh tool aims to stop deepfakes from being attributed to real artists

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as AI-generated slop continues to flood music streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name.
  • Spotify says the tool is designed to address a longstanding issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names.
  • The patch comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as AI-generated slop continues to flood music streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name. The official launch comes eight months after the company began beta testing the feature with select artists.

Spotify says the tool is designed to address a longstanding issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names.

The patch comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March.

With this fresh feature, Spotify is aiming to give artists more control over their digital identities as the volume of music uploaded to streaming services continues to grow.

Artists can enable the feature through Spotify for Artists to receive alerts when new music is submitted under their name. If a release doesn’t belong to them, they can remove their association with it to stop it from appearing on their profile.

By default, releases go live as scheduled unless an artist intervenes. If artists want greater control, they can choose to switch on an advanced setting that requires them to manually approve or reject releases before they appear on their profile.

In a recent development, “Artists should never have to find someone else’s music under their name, noted Sam Duboff. Spotify’s Global Head of Marketing and Policy, in an email, stated to TechCrunch. “Their artist profile should be in their control. Starting today, every artist on Spotify can use Artist Profile Protection to review what shows up on their profile and prevent spammy and incorrect releases from ever reaching their page or their fans. We’re the first and only streaming service with a solution to the industry-wide problem of content mismatch, and we hope it sets a new standard for streaming platforms.”.

The company notes it worked with thousands of artists during the beta testing phase to refine the tool and make it easier to protect their profiles without disrupting release schedules.

When Apple unveiled its inaugural folding phone, the iPhone Duo, it pretty much met expectations — but the biggest drawback was the company's decision to revert to Touch ID from Face ID, which felt like a huge step down for some.

However, the latest iOS 27.3 developer beta patches over this pain point, and owners of the Apple foldable can now unlock their devices with Face ID.

Industry observers note that for the most part, the iPhone Duo's fresh facial recognition tool functions very similarly to the Face ID feature we all know, allowing you to unlock your device from your lock screen. But because of the foldable's limited hardware support, it's not as robust as Face ID.

Before you get excited about the iPhone Duo's new software upgrade, there are a few limitations to bear in mind. Firstly, the camera-based facial recognition tool doesn't survive on its own, and still requires the help of Touch ID. If you want to unlock your iPhone Duo using facial recognition, it requires you to have recently used Touch ID or your device's passcode within a 45-minute window, so the two go hand-in-hand.

As far as the new facial recognition tool goes, it's only available to use on the Lock Screen, and doesn't have support for features like Apple Pay, passwords, logins, and other amenities that offer the same level of convenience. Presumably because of the Duo's folding hinge, numerous displays, and overall thinness, there's no room for a TrueDepth sensor, the dedicated tool that powers Face ID and all of its capabilities.

Still, it would've been the perfect opportunity for the firm to take inspiration from the likes of Google Pixel phones.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Though Google's smartphones also pack camera-based facial recognition, there's nothing that it can't do, be that making digital purchases, accessing passwords, signing into apps, and even organizing your photo gallery by the faces in each image.

It has been revealed that that said, while Pixel phones seem to have it all, camera-based facial recognition that's not supported by a sensor lacks a layer of security, making it much easier to bypass using 2D images of a subject. With sensor-based tools, it's much more difficult to achieve this, as they analyze and create a 3D map of the face, use detection tools to pick up facial liveliness, and pack infrared scattering tools so it can scan faces in darker environments.

It's still early days, however, and users are only just getting used to a world in which Apple foldables exist. It could be that we'll have to wait until the iPhone Duo's third-gen model to see some improvements on this front — which may not arrive until 2028 at the earliest, according to Bloomberg's own Mark Gurman.

#928. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.
  • It has been revealed that there are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses.
  • The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

It has been revealed that there are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

It has been revealed that I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

According to recent reports, emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

It has been revealed that what’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

It has been revealed that android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

It has been revealed that the Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

Sources indicate that the display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a massive movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

Recent findings suggest that when running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

According to recent reports, the display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

According to recent reports, the whole Aura interface feels upcoming-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

It has been revealed that there’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

According to recent reports, that’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

In a recent development, the puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

Sources indicate that I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

In a recent development, mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

According to recent reports, the refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I mentioned before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

It has been revealed that think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or introduces live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

In a recent development, speakers are embedded in the arms, pumping out audio that sounds as good as Xreal’s other glasses. Fine for games and movies, but you might prefer earbuds for isolation and privacy.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

It has been revealed that sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

Sources indicate that I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

Recent findings suggest that but what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

In a recent development, connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

According to recent reports, right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

It has been revealed that whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

Industry observers note that the glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

In a recent development, it’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

It has been revealed that this is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Sources indicate that xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

Recent findings suggest that right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

Sources indicate that the Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mac consumers will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.
  • Sources indicate that after sounding an alarm about the glitch last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the tech giant declared on its developer blog.
  • The concern rose to prominence in September, when Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mac consumers will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.

Sources indicate that after sounding an alarm about the glitch last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the tech giant declared on its developer blog. In its latest macOS beta, Apple introduced controls to ensure that customers will need to take "very explicit" actions to grant apps like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini "this extraordinary level of [full disk] access.".

The concern rose to prominence in September, when Inc. columnist Jason Aten noticed that Meta's Muse Mac app was able to access his messages even though he thought he had denied that permission. Meta argued that Aten must have granted access, saying the feature is entirely opt-in, but the incident caught Apple's eye. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems — including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history — without users' full knowledge and understanding," Apple wrote.

It has been revealed that apple vowed to address the concern with upcoming disk controls. As screen grabs from X user @madeby_ldt show, Apple's Full Disk Access setting now requires explicit permissions to be granted from a scary-looking pop-up screen. It states, "Your Mac will not be able to protect your data from [your desired AI app]," and forces you to review and OK the actions it will be able to take. Those include "Read, Change, Delete and Export all your Data," "View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos," and "View History and Browser as You.".

Industry observers note that the upcoming controls won't stop owners from granting AI agents access to your files, but it should give them pause. If one of those AI agents goes rogue — which is something we've seen before — they could potentially leak or misuse your private data. Stopping this is key for Mac models like the Studio that Apple is specifically marketing for local AI models and agents.

According to recent reports, "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring people clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy," Apple mentioned last month. The newly introduced feature is now out on macOS 27.3 beta 2, but there's no word on when it will be released to all users.

Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.

Nvidia said Tuesday that the fresh standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

According to recent reports, the Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce upcoming export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.

The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the tech giant to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.

In a recent development, the committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.

Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026.

Federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh said on Monday. They range from a broad growth boom to a downturn if the technology disappoints. He also told a Fed conference in San Francisco that AI gives upcoming power to bad actors.

Industry observers note that “SI empowers all, including bad actors. So, we’re thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their vulnerabilities,” Warsh stated.

Sources indicate that warsh opened the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted with the San Francisco Fed and livestreamed. He used “SI”, for super intelligence, throughout, the term the US government adopted after Trump’s executive order. The Fed has published his prepared remarks.

Industry observers note that the Board’s staff is using stylised, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios, Warsh noted. He called them illustrative, not forecasts or predictions.

In the first, AI raises productivity and the gains are shared between workers and the owners of capital. Real GDP grows above its long-run average and the US stays close to full employment.

In the second, growth still rises above average, but AI displaces jobs rather than complementing them. Automation and frictions in the labour market push unemployment above full-employment levels.

In the third, AI disappoints. After heavy investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and valuations could fall, leading to a slowdown and a rise in unemployment. The economy would recover, he mentioned, but without the productivity gains.

“Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders,” Warsh remarked.

Industry observers note that he did not comment on interest rates. He also did not address AI’s effect on inflation, as the Associated Press noted, though several Fed officials have tied the data centre buildout to rising prices.

Industry observers note that warsh then moderated a panel with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and Affirm CEO Max Levchin. Asked how worried people should be about cybersecurity, Arora remarked AI can now find flaws in code written over the past 50 years.

In a recent development, “It’s not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay,” Arora noted.

In a recent development, arora mentioned Mythos, which came out six months ago, is now within reach of most bad actors through open-source models. Outside security help is booked up, he said, because every company is fending off attempts to get into its systems. He called the next two to three years a “technology rebuild moment”.

Collison agreed. Even the Linux TCP stack, one of the most scrutinised pieces of software, turned out to be full of exploitable bugs, he said. Levchin called the attackers’ edge a temporary effect that would end in sturdier software.

It has been revealed that on jobs, Levchin said Affirm’s engineers are about five times more productive, with “zero layoffs due to AI”. Collison said Stripe is hiring far less for general and administrative roles but more engineers and salespeople. New businesses launching on Stripe each week are up about twofold year on year, he said.

US stocks extended an AI sell-off on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 3%, and selling picked up in the afternoon as investors took in Warsh’s comments, Business Insider reported. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, and Anthropic is due to price its IPO on Wednesday.

According to recent reports, TRMNL, the tech giant known for e-paper frames and kits, just debuted its biggest and most colorful product yet. Frame is a 31.5-inch full color e-paper display mounted in a handmade wooden frame, designed to show paintings, photos, maps, graphics and other still images in a more natural way than LCD or OLED screens. Though not cheap, it features high-quality materials and will be released in limited numbers to start with.

Recent findings suggest that if you've never heard of TRMNL, the tech giant has had some buzz of late with its e-paper displays sold in frames or kits. Thus far, products like the DIY (kit) and OG (picture frame) have been strictly black and white or grayscale, because "TRMNL is not a television. We avoid trying to do too much," founder Ryan Kulp explained in a blog post.

According to recent reports, however, the introduction of grayscale with the OG model apparently got the company thinking that color "aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even better," Kulp wrote. To that end, TRMNL introduced the full-color e-paper Frame, set to ship by late 2026 or early 2027 for $1,300 in a first batch of around 470 units.

"Over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display," Kulp wrote. "And yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure.".

To further improve picture quality, Frame will use clock sync to reduce flicker and extend battery life. Though internet connected, it offers a microSD port if you prefer to run it offline. Along with a rechargeable battery, you get a rear USB-C port with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. It can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation, and you can optionally buy or build your own kickstand.

Sources indicate that TRMNL is working on community developers on other features and even "created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform." The organization promises a transparent supply chain and has everything it needs to build Frame "in stock or on order" for a smooth fulfillment cycle. Everything is assembled by its team and not outsourced.

Sources indicate that pre-orders are now open starting at $1,300, with the first batch shipping to the USA, Canada, Mexico and Australia. Potential buyers outside those countries can still get in on the action by pre-ordering here, though the TRMNL said that "duty/import fees could be quite high given the product's customs value." Next year, it plans to open another woodworking shop near its Berlin warehouse to offer "postage- and duty-free fulfillment.".

#920. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1636 w)
