💡 Key Takeaways
  • Genesis AI co-founders Zhou Xian, left, and Théophile Gervet.
  • Genesis AI has raised $500m in a Series A round at a $3.5bn valuation, the Paris-based robotics startup said on Tuesday.
  • “We’re working to build the world’s best general-purpose robot, one that works reliably in the real world, day after day,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Genesis AI co-founders Zhou Xian, left, and Théophile Gervet.

Genesis AI has raised $500m in a Series A round at a $3.5bn valuation, the Paris-based robotics startup said on Tuesday. Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse co-led the round. Bloomberg first reported the talks back in July.

“We’re working to build the world’s best general-purpose robot, one that works reliably in the real world, day after day,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian stated.

Nvidia’s NVentures, AMD Ventures, Bpifrance, HSG, Samsung Next and Ericsson Ventures also took part, The Wall Street Journal reported. Angel investors include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Xavier Niel and former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn.

The money will fund building and deploying its robots, starting in factories and warehouses, Genesis said in its announcement. Zhou told Reuters it will also go into producing more Eno robots and expanding data collection and training.

Zhou and president Théophile Gervet, a former Mistral AI research scientist, founded the organization in 2024. It raised a $105m seed round in July 2025 and builds its own model, hardware and simulator.

In a recent development, its model, GENE, learns from people wearing sensor gloves, which Genesis claims map one to one onto its robot hands. More than 100 workers around the world wear the gloves and headset cameras, TechCrunch reported. The manufacturer also runs a simulator, Genesis World, to test the model across millions of scenarios.

Eno, its first robot, has two arms on a rotating wheeled base and no humanoid head.

“I don’t understand why robots need a head because … it doesn’t even have a brain living there,” Zhou told Reuters.

Genesis has built 30 to 40 Enos and is piloting them with a few undisclosed customers, TechCrunch reported. A contract manufacturer will start mass production in the US next year. Genesis is testing Eno with South Korea’s LG CNS in manufacturing and logistics. It expects a wider rollout in 2027, Reuters reported.

Zhou stated hardware is the main bottleneck. The company’s robot hands last only a few weeks of regular work before they need replacing, he told TechCrunch. In a demo for the outlet, Genesis’s model ran a pair of off-the-shelf arms. They packed and labelled a box on the first run, then fumbled on the second.

“I think next year, sometime next year, we’ll have a robotics model that just works out of the box,” Zhou told the Journal.

The round follows other large robotics raises this month, including Path Robotics, which raised $300m.

NC Band 2 is smaller, sleeker and has a longer battery life.

Recent findings suggest that natural Cycles is today announcing two new products; its second-generation fertility-tracking wearable, the NC Band 2, and its first ever smart ring, the NC Ring. The former is a refinement of last year's debut model, which has been redesigned to make it easier to wear. The latter shrinks down that same technology into a ring, albeit one that isn't going to be available in the US. If you're unfamiliar, Natural Cycles made its name with its FDA-cleared health app offering "digital birth control.".

Let's start with the Band 2. As before, it's a screen-free band, but with a raft of fit and finish tweaks made between the first and second generations. The older unit was designed to be worn only while sleeping, monitoring the wearer's heart rate, movement and temperature. Its successor, however, is a general-purpose activity tracker which can be worn day and night, adding additional insights into its user's health.

Industry observers note that the focus remains on fertility, and the band will interact directly with the Natural Cycles app offering personalized insights. Consumers can run one of five distinct modes: Birth Control, Blueprint Pregnancy, Follow Pregnancy, Postpartum and Perimenopause.

There have also been plenty of improvements to the hardware, with the Band 2 far smaller and lighter than its predecessor. Despite the smaller form factor and all-day wear, the battery life has increased from 14 days to 21. It's also a lot hardier, being able to withstand being immersed in water to depths of up to 50 meters.

Sources indicate that the upcoming NC Band 2 is available to pre-order today, priced at $149 alongside a year's app blueprint, or $99 for existing owners. It is HSA/FSA eligible and the company expects it to begin shipping at some point in December.

Industry observers note that of more interest, but not available in America, is the NC Ring, which begins shipping today in Canada, Europe and Australia. Measuring 2.43mm thick and 5.8mm wide, it's designed to keep an eye on its user's temperature and movement. It doesn't ship with an optical heart rate sensor both to reduce any night-time distractions and to keep the battery life running for up to 14 days on a charge. Like its wrist-worn siblings, it'll connect via Bluetooth to the Natural Cycles app to offer up more data for fertility and cycle tracking.

In a recent development, if you're wondering why Natural Cycles isn't selling the ring in the US, your guess is as good as ours. It certainly wouldn't do to speculate as to why it would choose to ignore such a lucrative and vast market. Apropos of nothing, Natural Cycles has a longstanding partnership with market leaders Oura, itself no stranger to using its patent library to shut down potential competitors.

Industry News: Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform.
  • The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.
  • The first significant caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

The first significant caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

When the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

Sources indicate that the big thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV indicates, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had complications with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

The other big use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Industry observers note that two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

That said, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

In a recent development, the glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

Sources indicate that the compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

Controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

In a recent development, the Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core issues facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a significant step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

#884. Router VPN vs. VPN app: How are these setups different?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (681 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Router VPN vs. VPN app: How are these setups different?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should you install a VPN on your router or your devices?
  • In a recent development, if you're a frequent VPN user, you may have an app installed on each one of your devices.
  • But even though a router-level VPN connection sounds like a good idea, it has its own set of drawbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Should you install a VPN on your router or your devices?

In a recent development, if you're a frequent VPN user, you may have an app installed on each one of your devices. But many routers these days have built-in support for VPN connections too. In theory, this means you can simply connect your router to the VPN and route internet traffic from every connected device on your network through the encrypted tunnel.

But even though a router-level VPN connection sounds like a good idea, it has its own set of drawbacks. While it can save you from managing individual connections, routing your household's internet traffic through a VPN on your router can lead to slower speeds.

It has been revealed that having noted that, not every device supports VPN connections, so tunneling your router is often your only option. That raises an key question: When does it make sense to use a VPN on your router, and when are individual apps the better option?

Recent findings suggest that there are good reasons to connect your router directly to a VPN instead of configuring each individual device. The first one is that you don't have to install apps on different devices, sign in to your account and remember to enable the tunnel every single time. Many of the best VPN services also restrict how many devices can connect at once. Your router takes up just one slot while routing traffic from all devices on your network through the VPN.

In a recent development, most VPN providers have dedicated apps for major operating systems including Windows, macOS, Android, iOS and even Linux. However, many devices that would benefit from a VPN connection, including game consoles like the Nintendo Switch and the PlayStation 5, don't offer support for it. Take smart TVs, for instance. Even though you might want to use a VPN for streaming apps like Netflix, many mainstream TV operating systems such as Samsung's Tizen and LG's webOS don't offer any VPN settings whatsoever. One of the ways to get around this would be to use a VPN-capable streaming device like an Nvidia Shield.

Finally, some routers have excellent VPN policy controls that allow you to selectively route certain website domains or devices through the encrypted tunnel. For example, you could choose to only route your smart TV's traffic or Netflix-related data through a VPN. Very few routers support this functionality, though.

Industry observers note that even with a router that has built-in VPN support, using a VPN directly on individual devices is often the better choice. If you mainly use a VPN to access geo-restricted content on streaming services like Netflix, or for the occasional task where connection security and privacy matter more than usual, a VPN app lets you select different locations and servers without affecting anyone else's connectivity in your household.

Many websites also block connections originating from VPN servers, which is why most people don't leave a VPN running at all times. For example, you may notice Google search often requires completing a CAPTCHA when you access it through a VPN. Other websites may fail to load entirely, leaving you with an HTTP 403 or 401 error. With a device-level connection, you can promptly disable the VPN to load a stubborn website.

Recent findings suggest that not every router is powerful enough to handle VPN encryption at high speeds. In practical terms, this means you may see a severe reduction in bandwidth with a VPN enabled on your router. Your smartphone or computer is significantly more powerful, so a device-level VPN connection can make full use of your internet connection instead of being bottlenecked to slower speeds.

While using a VPN on individual devices offers these advantages, note that each device takes up one connection slot, so you may want to keep the number of simultaneous connections down to a minimum. Leaving a VPN running all the time on your phone or laptop can also lead to battery drain, but with an app, you can switch it off whenever you don't need it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, noted it is a “pivotal time” for U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic U.S. House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

According to recent reports, rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, noted it is a “pivotal time” for U.S. climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman remarked.

President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the U.N. talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes and universities.

Huffman said the midterm election indicates that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Sources indicate that given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the U.S. from the U.N.’s climate framework, the extent of U.S. participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman noted that, in the past, U.S. congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman remarked in an interview with Inside Climate News.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman mentioned.

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners … and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

The upcoming Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the U.S. has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, mentioned U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

Industry observers note that “We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” noted Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

In a recent development, “I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the U.S. can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari stated.

“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are … supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”.

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”.

Singh said the U.S. has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the U.S. carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”.

In a recent development, singh stated until the U.S. pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”.

Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, stated the latest Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

According to recent reports, “What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping upcoming climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

Sources indicate that while meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible U.S. return to the climate talks.

Industry observers note that “The fact is the U.S. has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he remarked. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”.

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

Industry News: 5 notable Bose headphone settings that need to be manually turned on

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that pairing your Bose headphones is just the beginning.
  • Bose has made some of the most popular headphones around for years, but even if you've been using them for a while, you may not be getting everything you can out of yours.
  • Keep in mind that not every pair of Bose headphones will have access to all of these settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that pairing your Bose headphones is just the beginning. A few small tweaks in the companion app's settings can make your headphones feel more like yours.

Bose has made some of the most popular headphones around for years, but even if you've been using them for a while, you may not be getting everything you can out of yours. The tech giant's headphones are perfectly capable of producing great sound right out of the box, but some of their best features actually have to be activated manually. Whether there's something you always wished your headphones could do or you just want to see if they can perform even better, it's worth exploring settings like an equalizer, multi-connection support, noise canceling, shortcuts to your favorite features, or sidetone settings.

Keep in mind that not every pair of Bose headphones will have access to all of these settings. Newer QuietComfort models are upgraded in all the right places, offering a few unique features, while first-generation QuietComfort Ultra and QuietComfort headphones lack some of those features. You'll also need to download the Bose app to tweak anything beyond their basic settings, as the controls on the headphones themselves are pretty minimal.

According to recent reports, one useful feature on compatible Bose headphones is the equalizer (EQ). Like with any piece of audio equipment, the equalizer lets you modify different sound frequencies to your taste, like adjusting the audio quality in Apple Music, letting you pump up the bass or improving the high end so it's brighter. Reviews often call out Bose for boosting bass too much out of the box, so it may be a good idea to try turning it down a touch before making other adjustments.

Recent findings suggest that bose's equalizer only lets you change volume across three bands — bass, mid and treble — but that's plenty for most users without making it too complex. There are also preset options to choose from if you want to take Bose's recommendations or pick one to start with and customize your profile from there. You'll find the equalizer on the home screen of the Bose app, under EQ.

Industry observers note that one of the more annoying aspects of using Bluetooth headphones is having to disconnect and reconnect them whenever you want to switch from one device to another. Bluetooth multipoint lets Bluetooth devices connect to multiple sources at once, so you can switch between them without disconnecting and reconnecting. Compatible Bose headphones have this feature, but you have to enable it in the app.

You'll find Bluetooth multipoint in the Settings section of the app, under Bluetooth Connections. Just toggle it on, and you'll be able to connect your headphones to two different audio sources. To switch devices, pause the audio on one and press play on the other, or swap between them in the app if the switch doesn't happen. Like basically everything to do with Bluetooth, multipoint connection doesn't always work perfectly, but it's extremely convenient when it does.

Bose features some serious pros of using noise-canceling headphones. You can choose from a few modes to adjust how noise-canceling works, with newer models adding more modes. QuietComfort Ultra headphones turn on in Quiet mode by default, but if you find an option you like better, you can set the app to remember the last mode used through the app's Settings menu.

It has been revealed that under the Modes menu in the app, you'll find at least two different noise-canceling presets, depending on which headphones you have. Quiet (full noise cancellation) and Aware (full transparency) are available on the QuietComfort Ultra headphones. In newer headphones, Immersion mode aims to replicate the experience of music being played from a stage in front of you, and Cinema mode enhances dialogue clarity while you're watching movies and TV. You can also define multiple custom modes by choosing which specific noise-canceling features to activate.

Sources indicate that many Bose headphones let you customize their controls, though the specifics will obviously depend on which model you own. QuietComfort Ultra headphones have a touch-sensitive strip, and older headphone models offer the Action Button, both of which can activate your chosen shortcut.

Recent findings suggest that to set the behavior of the custom control, check the Shortcut option in the app. Depending on your model, this will let you choose from a few options, including hearing the battery level as it changes, changing the Immersive Audio mode and switching between previously connected Bluetooth devices. For headphones, you can only set one, but some earbuds let you assign a different shortcut to each ear. If you don't use shortcuts and don't want to risk accidentally activating them, you can also turn them off completely in the app.

Industry observers note that A somewhat more niche feature comes in the form of Self Voice. If you've ever taken a call while wearing headphones, especially noise-canceling ones, you might be familiar with how strange it can be to hear your own voice muffled as you speak. By default, Bose headphones feed a certain amount of your own voice back to you to make speaking feel more natural, otherwise known as sidetone.

Recent findings suggest that the Self Voice feature in the app lets you adjust just how much comes through, but you won't find it on the home screen. Instead, tap the Settings gear icon and look for Self Voice there, where you can set it to High, Medium or Low, or turn it off completely. As long as it's not turned off, Self Voice activates automatically during calls, so you don't need to manually toggle it on.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, with Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain consumers who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta is testing Direct, a newly introduced standalone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.

In a recent development, with Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain consumers who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought out various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.

Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the manufacturer says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.

The upcoming app also gives the firm a way to keep these owners within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem even if they don’t use Instagram itself.

Recent findings suggest that besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.

Meta says customers can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.

Sources indicate that meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.

The company also indicates it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young customers. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.

Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.

Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cameras don’t seem to reach the dizzying heights of last year’s 17 Ultra.

Xiaomi's premium smartphone series has been in great form in recent years. Alongside last year's 17 Ultra (and its Leica-collab camera), it rolled out its own passport-shaped foldable, the technically impressive 18 Fold, just before Apple debuted the iPhone Duo.

Its newly introduced phones, the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, combine a more advanced rear display with some of the tech giant's latest innovations found on the 17 Ultra and its foldables. Naturally, because it's 2026, that includes a serving of AI assistance and generative AI, but Xiaomi brought some genuinely smart ideas to the latter. The Pro series is launching in more regions this year, including the UK and other parts of Western Europe, but still won't come to the US. The 18 Pro Max is priced at £1400 (roughly $1,850) and the 18 Pro at £1,199 (around $1,580), continuing this year's upward trajectory of smartphone prices. Both are priced higher than Xiaomi's flagship (and my favorite camera phone), the 17 Ultra.

In a recent development, the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch main display and a slightly larger 2.9-inch rear display. The 18 Pro, meanwhile, has a 6.40-inch screen with a 2.7-inch rear display. The Pro Max model also features Snapdragon's new 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, with up to 16 gigs of RAM, while the 18 Pro has a (still powerful) Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 with 12GB of RAM.

There are also battery capacity differences between the two phones. The Xiaomi 18 Pro has a 6,000mAh cell with 90W max charging, but if you're demanding more battery life, the Pro Max has a larger 7,050mAh battery and 100W fast charging.

The hardware feels decidedly premium, complemented by a couple of vivid color options, including a gorgeous Velvet Red finish last seen on Xiaomi's latest foldable. Both phones will also come in Black, White and Cosmic Blue colors. Even if you choose the vivid red or blue models, it's the small back display that catches the eye first.

Recent findings suggest that the Back Display uses the same display tech as the Xiaomi 18 Pro series' screen, peaking at 4,000-nit brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates, though chances of seeing those upper limits are probably few and far between. Both the back display and camera array are protected with a single Corning Gorilla Glass Victus cover, making a surprisingly busy back look a little more cohesive.

The Back Display's functions fall into two main categories. First, like the flip foldables we've seen in recent years, it works as a display for the phone's primary cameras. The back display's viewfinder automatically switches to ultra-wide if it spots three or more people in the shot, but otherwise it's a stripped-down version of the camera app. While it makes sense, given the smaller screen space for buttons and modes, it relegates many shooting modes and features to the main camera app on the phone's main screen.

In a recent development, alongside the notifications and information feeds we've seen on phones like Samsung's Z Flip series and Motorola's Razr phones, including calls, maps and weather, Xiaomi adds a pin-to-back function that lets you attach text and images for quick reference. The manufacturer suggests pinning boarding passes and QR codes, but you could also add a cute pic of family or pets. It's also the first rear display to support apps like Spotify, YouTube Music and Google Maps – hopefully more apps will join those. Xiaomi remarked Gemini Live can run on the rear display, but I haven't been able to get it to work on my 18 Pro yet.

The new feature on this year's Back Display lets you program your own mini apps, similar to how you can program the iPhone's recent AI-infused Shortcuts. Using GenAI, you can describe a lightweight app or function, and the Xiaomi 18 Pro will attempt to make it a reality. It's a clever way to sidestep the difficulty of getting app developers on board with niche screen sizes and proportions. Xiaomi promises over 50 preset apps at launch, although the selection was much more limited on the Xiaomi 17 Pro I've been using.

According to recent reports, it's not about making dense, full-size apps, but rather simple, single-purpose (interactive) widgets. There's something to this idea, but I couldn't quite get apps to behave or look the way I wanted. One idea: a faux wallpaper that would generate screen cracks and glitches when touched. Regardless of how many times I asked the phone not to include an on-screen crack counter, ruining the appeal of my lame 'prank', subsequent vibe-coded builds still featured a counter.

I also tried to create a guess-the-flag quiz, but it seemed to lean heavily on the 25 or so countries that most of us could answer, easily. When I asked it to increase the flag range by 100 more, the phone struggled to generate a new mini app, even though I assumed it was an easy expansion of the initial premise. There are some smart implementations, including a button to 'polish' the idea you wrote to make it more palatable to generative AI.

It's a little sluggish to both refine and generate these mini-apps, especially if you've dipped your toe into genAI coding elsewhere, which is usually pretty swift. The feature requires an internet connection to work and it's not entirely clear whether they're generated on-device, which might explain slower processing.

Industry observers note that wallpaper options for the tiny rear display also include AI Group photo wallpapers, which I'm less sold on, which combine two different subjects into a group photo. You can even create composite portraits of celebrities and fictional characters – maybe this just isn't for me. I'll go back to my flag guessing.

Industry observers note that the primary screens on both phones feature Xiaomi's Privacy Display technology, which can be assigned to toggle on with specific apps (like banking apps, photo galleries, dating apps and more). This extends to notifications and even floating windows and split-screen versions of those apps — it's a better implementation of the privacy display tech we saw on Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra. In settings, you can even enable a gaze detection mode that notifies you if the front-facing camera recognizes someone possibly peering at your phone. The 18 Pro will notify you on-screen or with a more subtle vibration.

According to recent reports, cameras are once again a priority for Xiaomi. Both phones have dual 200-megapixel camera systems, with Leica Summilux lenses. The 18 Pro Max has a 200MP Light Fusion 960L primary sensor with LOFIC technology, which delivers more dynamic range to protect highlights and boost low-light performance. The 18 Pro, however, uses the same 200MP Light Fusion 960 sensor, minus the LOFIC part. Both have an f/1.67 lens and optical image stabilization.

The periscope telephoto is also 200MP, with an f/2.4 lens, OIS and 3.2x optical zoom, extending to 12.8x in-sensor cropped zoom. There's a 50MP ultrawide too, separately nestled below the other two cameras. This makes for a more sensible-looking camera array alongside the back display, the very opposite of Motorola's tryptophobia-inducing Signature 17.

Recent findings suggest that I've been testing the 18 Pro's cameras for only a few days (and the 18 Pro Max is arriving today, so I'll have updated impressions soon). Performance doesn't reach the high expectations set by last year's 17 Ultra, with its massive 1-inch sensor. While daylight shots and macro landscapes remain crisp, the standard Pro often struggled to capture moving subjects and low-light scenes. The Pro Max-exclusive LOFIC sensor could bridge that gap, however, so I'll upgrade this story if it does.

Leica's Essential Moments is an enjoyable shooting mode in the camera app, evolving from a single-camera mode to multiple styles and even lens options. It's a little different from the Leica camera simulations on Xiaomi's flagships last year. Powered by Xiaomi's own large model photography engine, the shooting mode applies one of three Leica-inspired color grades. You can also shoot through two "classic lens" simulations based on 35mm and 75mm lenses. Xiaomi has distilled it down to three styles, and I've always liked the old-school CCD tones of Leica cameras. As I've noted in other reviews and hands-ons, Xiaomi and Leica seem to have nailed this, including a monochrome mode (which, again, is great), while keeping it curated to just three distinct looks.

It has been revealed that there are all the other shooting modes you'd expect, too, with Xiaomi's pro shooting mode another standout. Focus peaking and exposure highlights are baked in, and you can refine your own filter parameters, including adding noise grain and hue.

Recent findings suggest that for now, Xiaomi's 17 Ultra remains its true photography flagship, but the 18 Pro series still delivers impressive results and, crucially, a fun shooting experience. In the UK, both phones are available to order from Xiaomi and Amazon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership revealed earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
  • Industry observers note that the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas.
  • Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership revealed earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

Industry observers note that the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline strategy to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

According to recent reports, uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a upcoming “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber noted that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal will offer drone delivery.

“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a fresh expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

Sources indicate that those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

Sources indicate that companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have mentioned.

And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the the communities where they services are available.

Recent findings suggest that zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based firm’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

It has been revealed that uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither tech giant has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global and that included backing by Uber, among others.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of us use Google Maps the same way day in and day out — we type in an address, follow the instructions and arrive at our destination.
  • None of these features require a newly introduced app or a subscription, either.
  • According to recent reports, there's a feature within Google Maps that lets you specify what car you're driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maps has more tricks than you’ve tapped.

Most of us use Google Maps the same way day in and day out — we type in an address, follow the instructions and arrive at our destination. But the app also offers a lot of useful tools that aren't as easily accessible as telling it where to go. If you want to set a reminder for when to leave or ensure your music is uninterrupted while still getting the step-by-step instructions, there are settings you can change to make that happen. You can also turn Google Maps into a much more useful tool if you tell it what type of car you have, or specify your route settings all so you can get customized recommendations.

None of these features require a newly introduced app or a subscription, either. They are built directly into Google Maps, and you can get to them with a little bit of digging around, especially when you know where to look.

According to recent reports, there's a feature within Google Maps that lets you specify what car you're driving. The make and model don't matter as much as what type of engine it has, letting you choose between gas, diesel, hybrid and electric. With this info, the app can tailor routing decisions to your car's needs.

Sources indicate that for EV and plug-in hybrid owners, this feature is worth considering because you can tell Google Maps exactly what type of plug or adapter your car requires. This allows Maps to automatically surface compatible charging stations. You can find this setting in Settings > Your vehicles. Once set, you can search for charging stations along your route, and the app will signal those that will work with your specific car.

In a recent development, route preferences deserve the same attention. The app's settings make it possible to toggle options to avoid tolls, ferries or even highways. This is useful if you'd rather take the scenic (or cheaper) route or if you wish to avoid the freeway at its higher speeds. To turn the feature on, go to Settings > Navigation, and you'll find all toggles under Route options. One thing that will save you time in the long run is setting or changing your home address on Google Maps so you can jump straight to your custom directions with a single tap. If you have your Gemini assistant enabled, you can even say "navigate home" and it will set the route for you.

Recent findings suggest that running late is rarely about the drive itself, but more about leaving at the wrong time. Unless an accident has delayed your journey, you probably left home late in accordance with your predicted arrival time — Google Maps is that good at estimating when you'll arrive based on your chosen route.

Well, you can use Google Maps on iPhone and its "Set a reminder to leave" feature to receive an alert telling you when to head out so you're not late for appointments. You can set an arrive-by time (or a leave-by time) for your destination under Directions > transportation mode and then tap the three-dot menu and select Set a reminder to leave > Depart or Arrive > set the time > Done. Maps will now notify you when to leave. On Android, things are a little different; to get the same results requires Google Calendar to set the reminder by creating an event with the appointment's date and time while adding the destination to the location field.

It has been revealed that this feature shines best in busy cities where traffic on the same stretch of road can vary dramatically between a Monday afternoon and a Friday evening. For anyone juggling back-to-back meetings, school pickups and a million extracurricular activities, these reminders remove the need to check the app constantly. It's a quiet but dependable feature, and it's equally useful if you're planning on using public transport.

According to recent reports, if you've ever had Spotify, a book or a podcast cut out midway to announce an upcoming exit, you know how annoying that can be. Thankfully, there's an easy fix if you'd like to silence Google Maps: you simply have to turn off the "Play voice over Bluetooth" setting, a fine way to improve your Android Auto experience. This will stop Google Maps from interrupting your music over your car's speakers, while still giving you visual turn-by-turn guidance on screen. The voice telling you to turn left or right will come from your phone rather than your car's speakers. It's a small adjustment that will make a substantial difference, especially if you drive in the city a lot and need to change direction often. To do this, go to your profile, scroll down to Settings and go to Navigation. The feature's toggle will be available up top, under Sound & Voice.

It has been revealed that one cool perk that's worth knowing about when you're using Android Auto is that when you're parked at your destination or somewhere for a rest, you can take a breather and play games directly on an Android Auto screen. That could make the wait during your kid's next practice session a little more entertaining.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected ….
  • The organization stated at the time that it was a technical concern and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The organization has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected ….

The organization stated at the time that it was a technical concern and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs confirmed the previous month.

People were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f.

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In a recent development, in less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two complications. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

According to recent reports, A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […].

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The patch went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent glitch because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the upgrade wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you're making a chocolate ganache for your holiday party, and instead of a glossy glaze, you’re staring at a curdled mess. To get help in the moment, tap the Live icon in the Google app (available on Android and iOS), turn on your video, and point your camera at the mixing bowl. You can then use your voice to ask Search if the chocolate is salvageable and get instructions for an easy fix, along with links to explore further.

When you spot holiday decor inspiration, like an eye-catching tablescape at a local restaurant or a festive design online, Lens helps you bring the look home. Then ask, “help me find the pieces to recreate this tablescape for my holiday party next weekend.”.

Apple has released the second iOS 27.3 developer beta for iPhone. The upcoming software update includes the redesigned Health app, new Safari features, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and more.

The second beta follows the first developer release on November 3 and first public beta on November 5.

One of the biggest changes introduced in iOS 27.3 so far is the redesigned Health app, which briefly appeared during iOS 27.2 testing before being removed ahead of release.

On supported iPhones, Health’s fresh Insights tab brings together trends from sleep, activity, and more. A new Longevity tab includes Health Age, which uses Apple Watch data to compare your health metrics with what’s typical for your age.

Our full iOS 27.3 beta 1 roundup covers additional changes, including expanded Siri AI language support and Apple Music updates.

Recent findings suggest that update, 6:15 p.m. ET: Apple has now released beta 2 for tvOS 27.3 (24K5298d) and HomePod 27.3 (24K5298d).

Recent findings suggest that apple has just released beta 2 for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and more. It’s available for developers, but a public beta will likely follow in the next couple days.

Two weeks ago Apple introduced an exciting wave of beta updates as iOS 27.3 and companion releases introduced many new features.

Recent findings suggest that siri AI upgrades are a significant focus in 27.3, with latest languages, Siri Recap, and advanced in-app actions. There’s also a preview of new third-party app capabilities for Siri.

The all-new Health app has returned in iOS and iPadOS 27.3, this time with the expectation of launching in the public release. Fitness also adds a new Gym Strength program.

Recent findings suggest that apple Music now has a Selfie Sing feature for creating personal karaoke videos, and an improved lyrics view. Safari adds Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more.

Recent findings suggest that that’s just a sampling of the upcoming features in beta 1. And now today, beta 2 is here for iPadOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, visionOS 27.3, and more.

We’re expecting to see additional new features and refinements today, like video podcasts being added to the Apple TV app. We’ll keep you posted on everything noteworthy we discover.

watchOS 27.3 has one of my personal favorite new features in Siri Recap, so I’m curious to see if Apple keeps refining the experience throughout the beta in response to user feedback.
